title: Emergency Numbers and What to Do in a Disaster
summary: Two numbers, one question you will be asked first, and a payphone trick that works without money. Read this before you need it, not while you need it.
body_html:
You will not be reading a webpage when this matters. So the useful thing is to know the first thirty seconds of each call, and one detail about payphones that almost nobody knows.

The numbers, and the question you get asked first

For sudden illness, injury or fire, dial 119. [source:1] For a traffic accident, a crime, or any situation where you need a police officer to come immediately, dial 110. [source:1]

Here is the part worth rehearsing. When you call 119, the operator asks whether it is a fire or an ambulance. [source:1] You answer with one of two phrases — "kyūkyū desu" for an ambulance, or "kaji desu" for a fire. [source:1]

That question comes first, before anything else. If you are expecting to start by explaining the situation, the call stalls at the opening exchange.

After that, for an ambulance: the place you want the ambulance to come to and a landmark, then the patient's symptoms and age, then your name and contact details. [source:1] For a fire: the location of the fire, then your name and contact details. [source:1]

The agency links a multilingual site explaining how to call an ambulance. [source:1] Look at it once now, while you are calm.

For a police call, the operator will mainly ask: when and where and what happened; your name and contact details; the other party's or suspect's sex, number, age and clothing; and whether anyone is injured. [source:1]

And if you cannot make the call yourself, ask someone nearby for help. [source:1] That line is in the official guidebook, which tells you it is a normal thing to do rather than a failure.

The payphone detail

This is the single most useful thing on this page, because it works when your phone does not — no battery, no signal, no credit, lost phone.

You can make emergency calls from a public payphone, and coins and a phone card are not needed. [source:1] The guidebook lists three numbers for this: the police, the coast guard, and the fire service. [source:1] The coast guard one is the one nobody has heard of — worth knowing if your school is coastal or you take a ferry.

How, depending on the phone:

  • If the payphone has a red emergency button: lift the receiver, press the emergency button, then dial. [source:1]
  • If it has no emergency button: lift the receiver and dial directly. [source:1]

Payphones have become scarce but they have not disappeared, and this is precisely the situation they still exist for. Notice where the one nearest your home and your school is. It takes one walk.

Rain, floods and landslides

The guidebook explains why Japan's rain is different from rain where you grew up, and it is worth understanding rather than memorising.

Heavy rain often falls when warm southern air and cold northern air stall along a front over Japan at the turn of the seasons, and widely when a typhoon or a low pressure system with a front passes nearby. [source:1] Terrain can drive strong updrafts so that developed cumulonimbus clouds form one after another over the same place, which is how rain keeps falling in the same area. [source:1]

Two things result. Rivers flood, which can submerge buildings and sweep people away. [source:1] And landslides occur when rain or an earthquake collapses hillsides, or when earth, rocks and trees mixed with water flow out of a river — destroying or burying buildings and blocking roads. [source:1]

The preparation that actually matters

One task, done once, before anything happens.

Use a hazard map to check which places near you are at risk of flooding or landslides, where the evacuation site is, and a safe route from your home to it. [source:1] Hazard maps and evacuation sites are published on each municipality's website. [source:1]

Do this in your first weeks, at the same time as your address registration. You will be at the municipal office anyway.

When evacuation information is issued

Evacuation information is issued to urge evacuation when a disaster is likely or has occurred. [source:1] When your municipality issues it, you move from the dangerous place to a safe one. [source:1]

One of the levels, "evacuation of older people and others", is information urging those who need more time to evacuate — older people and small children among them — to start leaving dangerous places. [source:1]

And the judgement call the guidebook makes explicitly, which is the most humane line in it: if a flood has already begun and going to the evacuation site would itself be dangerous, flee somewhere else safe instead — a nearby sturdy building, or if even that is difficult, the 2nd floor or higher of your home — taking whatever action protects your life. [source:1]

Read that as permission. The official advice is not "reach the designated site or fail". It is "get to the safest place you can actually reach".

One Japan-specific thing

Volcanic alert levels are issued so that dangerous places and the action to take are immediately clear, and they are published for Japan's active volcanoes. [source:1] They run from merely noting that a mountain is an active volcano, through restrictions around the crater and a ban on climbing, to evacuation of those living in dangerous places. [source:1]

If you plan to hike, the guidebook also says to check eruption warnings and the hazard map, submit a climbing plan, and prepare a communication device and a helmet. [source:1]

Do these five things this month

  • Save 119 and 110 in your phone, and learn the two reply phrases. [source:1]
  • Watch the multilingual ambulance-call explainer once. [source:1]
  • Find your nearest payphone, and remember that emergency calls from it need no coins or card. [source:1]
  • Download your municipality's hazard map and walk the route to your evacuation site once. [source:1]
  • Tell one person at your school where you live. If you cannot make the call yourself, someone needs to know.

The guidebook this page draws on is published free in multiple languages and covers far more than emergencies — see the official guidebook nobody tells you about. For the everyday rules that cause more routine trouble, see daily life rules. For the arrival paperwork to do first, see your first week in Japan.

This page summarises the Immigration Services Agency's guidebook, which is linked below and is the authority; it reflects systems as at a stated date and is revised. Municipal procedures and hazard maps differ by area. In an actual emergency, call — do not read.

claims_without_sources: 「kyūkyū desu」「kaji desu」というローマ字表記 —— ガイドブックは「救急です。」「火事です。」と日本語で書いており、ローマ字綴りは当方が読者のために付けたもの。発音の便宜であって出典の表記ではない。
公衆電話が減っているという記述 —— 一般的に知られた事実だが、ガイドブックの記述ではなく統計も確認していない。「減ったが無くなっていない」という程度に留めた。
警戒レベル4・5の内容 —— ガイドブックには記載があるが本記事では確認した範囲（レベル3）のみを引いた。レベルを不完全に並べると読者が自分の該当レベルを誤認するため、代わりに「自治体が避難情報を出したら避難する」という原則を前に置いた。
地震への備え（家具固定・備蓄等）—— ガイドブックに地震の節があるが本記事では内容を確認していないため触れていない。別記事で扱う余地がある。
避難場所と避難所の違い —— 日本の制度上区別があるが、ガイドブックの当該箇所から確認していないため用語を区別して書いていない。
緊急通報が無料である範囲（携帯電話からの場合等）—— 出典は公衆電話について硬貨・テレホンカードが不要と述べており、他の回線については述べていない。公衆電話に限定して書いた。
